prompt: A command produces results and also produces a warning. Do the two travel on the same channel?
optionA: Yes; everything a command produces travels together
optionB: No; results go on the ordinary output channel and warnings on the error channel
optionC: Yes, unless the command is told otherwise
optionD: No; warnings are not produced by commands at all
correctAnswerText: No; results go on the ordinary output channel and warnings on the error channel
explanation: Two separate outgoing channels exist and both are shown on the screen by default. Sharing a screen is what makes them look like one.

prompt: How many channels does a command typically have?
optionA: One, used for everything
optionB: Two, one in and one out
optionC: Four, one for each kind of message
optionD: Three: one incoming and two outgoing
correctAnswerText: Three: one incoming and two outgoing
explanation: Input arrives on one channel and output leaves on two, separated into ordinary results and errors. The separation is what makes the two independently routable.

prompt: A command reports that a file could not be opened. Which channel carries that message?
optionA: The error channel
optionB: The ordinary output channel
optionC: The incoming channel
optionD: Neither; failures are not written to a channel
correctAnswerText: The error channel
explanation: Anything reporting that something went wrong belongs on the error channel. Keeping it apart is what lets results be captured cleanly.

prompt: Why are results and errors kept on separate channels?
optionA: So that errors can be displayed in a different colour
optionB: So that errors are produced faster
optionC: So that results can be sent somewhere without the errors going with them
optionD: So that a command can produce only one of the two
correctAnswerText: So that results can be sent somewhere without the errors going with them
explanation: Separation exists to make the two routable independently. Capturing results into a file while still seeing problems on the screen is the everyday consequence.

prompt: A user watching a terminal sees results and an error message appear together and concludes they are on one channel. What is wrong with the conclusion?
optionA: Nothing; appearing together means one channel
optionB: Both channels point at the screen by default, which is why they appear together
optionC: The error must have been written to the output channel by mistake
optionD: The two appeared together by coincidence
correctAnswerText: Both channels point at the screen by default, which is why they appear together
explanation: The screen is the default destination for both, so the evidence is consistent with either account. Sending one of them elsewhere is what makes the separation visible.

prompt: A command output is sent to a file instead of the screen. What appears on the screen?
optionA: The output, as well as going to the file
optionB: A summary of the output
optionC: The output, delayed until the command finishes
optionD: Nothing from the ordinary output channel
correctAnswerText: Nothing from the ordinary output channel
explanation: Redirecting moves the output rather than copying it. The screen sees none of what went to the file.

prompt: A command that produces no output at all has its output redirected to a new file. Is the file created?
optionA: Yes, and it is empty
optionB: No, since there was nothing to write
optionC: No, and the command fails
optionD: Yes, containing a message saying there was no output
correctAnswerText: Yes, and it is empty
explanation: The file is prepared before the command runs, so it exists whether or not anything is written. That preparation is what makes the emptying behaviour matter.

prompt: What does redirecting a command output achieve?
optionA: It saves a copy while still showing it
optionB: It changes what the command produces
optionC: It sends that channel to a file rather than to the screen
optionD: It makes the command run faster
correctAnswerText: It sends that channel to a file rather than to the screen
explanation: The destination changes and the content does not. The command behaves identically and its output ends up somewhere else.

prompt: A user redirects a command output to a file and is surprised to see a message still appear on the screen. What is the explanation?
optionA: The redirection failed
optionB: The message was on the error channel, which was not redirected
optionC: The file was full
optionD: The command wrote the message twice
correctAnswerText: The message was on the error channel, which was not redirected
explanation: Only the ordinary output channel was sent to the file. Errors continue to the screen unless they are redirected as well.

prompt: Two commands are joined by a pipe. What does the second receive?
optionA: The name of the first command as an argument
optionB: The errors produced by the first
optionC: Nothing; the two simply run one after the other
optionD: The ordinary output of the first, as its incoming channel
correctAnswerText: The ordinary output of the first, as its incoming channel
explanation: The pipe connects one outgoing channel to the next incoming one. The second command reads it as though it were typed in.

prompt: Do errors from the first command travel down a pipe to the second?
optionA: No; a pipe carries the ordinary output channel only
optionB: Yes; everything the first produces is passed on
optionC: Yes, but only if the first command fails
optionD: No; errors stop the pipeline entirely
correctAnswerText: No; a pipe carries the ordinary output channel only
explanation: The error channel is not what the pipe connects, so errors go to the screen as usual. This is why an error can appear while the pipeline continues.

prompt: Three commands are joined by two pipes. What does the third receive?
optionA: The output of the first
optionB: The outputs of the first and second combined
optionC: The output of the second
optionD: The original input to the first
correctAnswerText: The output of the second
explanation: Each pipe connects one stage to the next, so each stage sees only what its immediate predecessor produced.

prompt: A user pipes a command output into a second command and finds the second acting on nothing. The first produced only errors and no ordinary output. Why did the second receive nothing?
optionA: The pipe was written incorrectly
optionB: Errors do not travel down a pipe, and there was no ordinary output to send
optionC: The second command cannot read from a pipe
optionD: The first command finished too quickly
correctAnswerText: Errors do not travel down a pipe, and there was no ordinary output to send
explanation: The first command did produce something and put it on the channel the pipe does not carry. The second correctly received an empty input.

prompt: A file of ten lines is fed into a stage that keeps only lines containing the word error, and three lines contain it. That stage output goes to a stage that counts lines. What does the counting stage receive?
optionA: Ten lines
optionB: Seven lines
optionC: One line
optionD: Three lines
correctAnswerText: Three lines
explanation: The counting stage sees what reached it, which is what the filter let through. The original ten are no longer available to it.

prompt: Twenty lines are fed through a stage keeping only lines containing "warn", which passes eight, and then through a stage keeping only lines containing "disk", which passes two of those eight. What does a fourth stage receive?
optionA: Two lines
optionB: Twenty lines
optionC: Eight lines
optionD: Ten lines
correctAnswerText: Two lines
explanation: Each stage narrows what the next one sees, so the fourth receives what survived both filters. The counts at earlier points are not recoverable later in the chain.

prompt: A file already contains fifty lines. A command producing three lines has its output redirected into that file in the replacing form. What does the file contain afterwards?
optionA: Fifty-three lines
optionB: The fifty original lines only
optionC: The three new lines only
optionD: The three new lines followed by the fifty original ones
correctAnswerText: The three new lines only
explanation: The replacing form empties the file first. Adding to the end is a different form that would have given fifty-three.

prompt: A file contains a week of records. A command that turns out to produce no output at all has its output redirected into that file in the replacing form. What does the file contain afterwards?
optionA: The week of records, since the command wrote nothing
optionB: Nothing; it was emptied before the command ran and nothing replaced the contents
optionC: The week of records, plus an empty line
optionD: Nothing, and the file no longer exists
correctAnswerText: Nothing; it was emptied before the command ran and nothing replaced the contents
explanation: Emptying happens as the redirection is set up rather than as output arrives. A command that produces nothing still destroys what was there.

prompt: A command output is redirected to a log file. The command produces an error. Where does the error appear?
optionA: In the log file, with the output
optionB: Nowhere; it is discarded
optionC: In a separate file created automatically
optionD: On the screen
correctAnswerText: On the screen
explanation: Only the ordinary output channel was redirected. The error channel still points at the screen.

prompt: A scheduled job runs with its output redirected to a log and nobody watching the screen. It fails with an error. Where does the error go?
optionA: To wherever the error channel points, which is not the log
optionB: Into the log, alongside the output
optionC: To the person who scheduled the job
optionD: Nowhere; scheduled jobs produce no errors
correctAnswerText: To wherever the error channel points, which is not the log
explanation: The redirection covered one channel and the job has no screen. Capturing the error channel as well is what makes a scheduled job diagnosable.

prompt: A team investigates a failure and finds their log file contains the output up to the point of failure and no explanation of it. Only the ordinary output channel was redirected into the log, and the explanation was produced on the error channel. Why is the explanation missing?
optionA: The command failed before it could write the explanation
optionB: The log file was truncated at the point of failure
optionC: It went to the error channel, which was never redirected into the log
optionD: The command produced no explanation at all
correctAnswerText: It went to the error channel, which was never redirected into the log
explanation: The log is complete for what it was told to capture. Directing the error channel to the same file is what would have included the reason.

prompt: The lines "apple", "banana", "apricot" and "cherry" pass through a stage that keeps only lines beginning with the letter a, and then through a stage that converts to upper case. What emerges?
optionA: apple and apricot
optionB: APPLE and APRICOT
optionC: APPLE, BANANA, APRICOT and CHERRY
optionD: APPLE only
correctAnswerText: APPLE and APRICOT
explanation: Two lines survive the filter and both are then converted. The order of the two stages gives filtered-then-converted rather than the reverse.

prompt: The lines "10", "3", "7" and "22" pass through a stage that keeps only lines of exactly one character, and then through a stage that sorts. What emerges?
optionA: 3, 7, 10 and 22 in order
optionB: 10, 3, 7 and 22 unchanged
optionC: 7 and 3, in that order
optionD: 3 and 7, in that order
correctAnswerText: 3 and 7, in that order
explanation: Only the two single-character lines survive, and sorting them puts 3 before 7. The two-digit lines never reach the sorting stage.

prompt: Six lines pass through a stage that removes duplicates, leaving four, and then through a stage that keeps only lines containing the letter x, of which three of the original six qualified and two survived the deduplication. Each stage acts on what the previous stage produced rather than on the original six. What emerges?
optionA: Two lines
optionB: Three lines
optionC: Four lines
optionD: Six lines
correctAnswerText: Two lines
explanation: The filter sees the deduplicated four rather than the original six, so two qualify. Applying the filter to the original set would have given three.

prompt: A file of one hundred lines is filtered to those containing the word failed, and the result is counted. The count reads twelve. What does twelve refer to?
optionA: The lines in the file
optionB: The lines not containing the word
optionC: The lines containing the word failed
optionD: The number of times the word appears
correctAnswerText: The lines containing the word failed
explanation: The counting stage counts what reached it, which is what the filter passed. The size of the original file is no longer visible at that point.

prompt: A line contains the word failed three times. A pipeline filters for that word and counts lines. How much does that line contribute to the count?
optionA: Three, once for each occurrence
optionB: One, since the stage counts lines rather than occurrences
optionC: Nothing, since duplicates within a line are ignored
optionD: It cannot be determined
correctAnswerText: One, since the stage counts lines rather than occurrences
explanation: Filtering keeps the line once and counting counts lines. Counting occurrences would need a different stage.

prompt: A pipeline filters a log for errors, removes duplicate lines, and counts what remains, giving four. A team reports that four errors occurred. Duplicate lines were removed before the count, so identical errors occurring many times contribute one each. What does four actually count?
optionA: Four error occurrences in total
optionB: Four lines in the original log
optionC: Four different files containing errors
optionD: Four distinct error lines, however many times each occurred
correctAnswerText: Four distinct error lines, however many times each occurred
explanation: The deduplication stage is what separates the two readings. One error repeated a thousand times contributes one to this figure.

prompt: A stage in the middle of a pipeline receives lines. Can it tell which file they came from?
optionA: No; it receives the lines and nothing about their origin
optionB: Yes; the file name travels with the lines
optionC: Yes, if the first stage read a file
optionD: Only if the pipeline has exactly two stages
correctAnswerText: No; it receives the lines and nothing about their origin
explanation: A stage sees the content arriving on its incoming channel and nothing else. Including the file name in the content is what makes it available.

prompt: The same filtering stage is used once with its output going to the screen and once with its output going to a file. Does it behave differently?
optionA: Yes; it produces less output when writing to a file
optionB: Yes; it formats differently for a file
optionC: No; it produces the same output either way
optionD: Only if the file already exists
correctAnswerText: No; it produces the same output either way
explanation: A stage does not know where its output is going, so it cannot behave differently. Some tools do adjust their formatting when writing to a screen, and that is a deliberate feature rather than the general rule.

prompt: A team wants a middle stage in a pipeline to behave differently when it is the last stage. A stage receives its input and produces its output without any information about what comes after it. What follows?
optionA: It can, by checking whether its output goes to a screen
optionB: It cannot, since nothing tells a stage what follows it
optionC: It can, by counting the stages in the pipeline
optionD: It can, by asking the previous stage
correctAnswerText: It cannot, since nothing tells a stage what follows it
explanation: Independence from context is what makes stages composable at all. Passing the intention in as a setting is how the requirement actually gets met.

prompt: A command can be given a file as a named target, or the same file can be supplied on its incoming channel. What is the difference from the command point of view?
optionA: There is no difference at all
optionB: In one case the content arrives faster
optionC: In one case the content is read-only
optionD: In one case it knows the file name and in the other it receives only the contents
correctAnswerText: In one case it knows the file name and in the other it receives only the contents
explanation: The contents are identical and the knowledge of where they came from is not. That is why one form can report a file name in its output and the other cannot.

prompt: A command that normally prints the file name alongside each matching line is given its input on the incoming channel instead of as a named file. What happens to the file names in its output?
optionA: They are absent, since the command was never told a name
optionB: They appear as before
optionC: They appear as the word input
optionD: The command refuses to run
correctAnswerText: They are absent, since the command was never told a name
explanation: The command cannot report what it was not given. Supplying the file as a named target is what restores the names.

prompt: A script searches several files and reports which file each match came from. A colleague rewrites it to feed the files in on the incoming channel instead. The rewritten form supplies only the contents, so the command is never told which file a line came from. What is lost?
optionA: Nothing; the same matches are found either way
optionB: The matches themselves, since the search cannot work this way
optionC: The file names, since the command receives contents with no indication of their source
optionD: The order of the results
correctAnswerText: The file names, since the command receives contents with no indication of their source
explanation: The same lines are found and their provenance is not. Naming the files as targets is what keeps the report usable.

prompt: A pipeline of four stages produces nothing. How should the responsible stage be found?
optionA: Rewrite the pipeline from scratch
optionB: Run the first stage alone, then the first two, and so on until the output disappears
optionC: Assume the last stage is at fault, since it produced the empty result
optionD: Check whether the input file exists and stop there
correctAnswerText: Run the first stage alone, then the first two, and so on until the output disappears
explanation: Stopping at each point shows where the content is lost. The last stage produced the visible empty result and need not be the stage that emptied it.

prompt: A pipeline produces nothing. Running the first two stages alone produces forty lines, and running the first three produces nothing. The output survives two stages and disappears after the third. Which stage is responsible?
optionA: The fourth, since the pipeline ends with no output
optionB: The first, since it read the input
optionC: The second, since it passed forty lines
optionD: The third, since the content was present before it and absent after
correctAnswerText: The third, since the content was present before it and absent after
explanation: Bisecting the pipeline locates the loss precisely. The fourth stage received nothing and had nothing to lose.

prompt: A user saw an error on screen while a command output was being written to a file. The file does not contain the error. Why not?
optionA: The error travelled on a channel that was not being written to the file
optionB: The file was written before the error occurred
optionC: The error was too long to fit
optionD: The command removed the error from the file
correctAnswerText: The error travelled on a channel that was not being written to the file
explanation: What went to the file is what was redirected there. The screen showed the other channel, which nothing captured.

prompt: A pipeline captures its final output to a file. A stage in the middle produces an error, which appears on the screen. The team expected it in the file. A pipe carries only the ordinary output channel, so a middle stage error never enters the pipeline. Why is it not in the file?
optionA: The error was overwritten by later output
optionB: The final stage discarded it
optionC: The error never entered the pipeline, so it could not reach the file at the end of it
optionD: The file captured only the last stage output and the error came from an earlier one
correctAnswerText: The error never entered the pipeline, so it could not reach the file at the end of it
explanation: Each stage error channel goes to the screen independently of the pipe. Redirecting each stage error channel, or the whole pipeline, is what captures them.

prompt: A pipeline filters lines containing a word and then counts them. The two stages are swapped so that counting comes first. What changes?
optionA: Nothing; the same number is produced
optionB: The result becomes the count of all lines rather than of the matching ones
optionC: The result becomes zero
optionD: The filter stops working
correctAnswerText: The result becomes the count of all lines rather than of the matching ones
explanation: Counting first produces a single number, which the filter then examines. The filter is looking at a count rather than at the lines.

prompt: A pipeline sorts lines and then removes duplicates. A colleague swaps the two so that duplicates are removed first. Removing duplicates does not depend on the order lines arrive in, and sorting does not depend on whether duplicates are present. Does the result change?
optionA: Yes; duplicates can only be removed from sorted input
optionB: Yes; the output will be unsorted
optionC: Yes; some duplicates will survive
optionD: No; the two stages commute here and the final set of lines is the same
correctAnswerText: No; the two stages commute here and the final set of lines is the same
explanation: Neither stage needs what the other provides, so the order is free. Some tools remove only adjacent duplicates, which would make sorting a prerequisite, and this stem describes one that does not.

prompt: A pipeline takes the first ten lines and then filters for a word, producing two results. Swapping the two stages produces ten results. Taking the first ten before filtering limits the filter to those ten, while filtering first lets the whole input be searched. Which order answers the question "what are the first ten matching lines"?
optionA: Filtering first, then taking ten, since the ten must be chosen from the matches
optionB: Taking ten first, then filtering, since ten is the limit
optionC: Either; both produce the first ten matching lines
optionD: Neither; the question needs a different pipeline
correctAnswerText: Filtering first, then taking ten, since the ten must be chosen from the matches
explanation: The two orders answer different questions, and only one of them is the question asked. Taking ten first answers "how many of the first ten match".

prompt: A pipeline processes a very large file. One stage filters out ninety per cent of the lines and one stage is slow and expensive per line. The expensive stage costs the same per line wherever it sits, and the filter reduces the number of lines reaching whatever follows it. Where should the expensive stage go?
optionA: Before the filter, so that no line is missed
optionB: Either; the total work is the same
optionC: After the filter, so that it processes a tenth as many lines
optionD: Before the filter, so that the filter sees processed lines
correctAnswerText: After the filter, so that it processes a tenth as many lines
explanation: Both orders give the same result here and not the same cost. Where the expensive stage changes what the filter would match, the orders stop being interchangeable and the cost argument no longer applies.

prompt: A team moves a filtering stage earlier in a pipeline for speed, and the results change. The stage that used to run before the filter altered the lines in a way that affected whether the filter matched them. Why did the results change?
optionA: Moving a stage earlier always changes the results
optionB: The filter now sees the unaltered lines, and it matches them differently
optionC: The pipeline became too fast for the filter
optionD: The filter was damaged by the move
correctAnswerText: The filter now sees the unaltered lines, and it matches them differently
explanation: Reordering is free only when neither stage affects what the other does. Here one stage was changing the very text the filter examines.

prompt: A team needs the number of distinct users appearing in a log. Each line names one user and a user may appear many times. Users repeat across lines and the requirement is a count of distinct users rather than of lines. Which pipeline fits?
optionA: Extract the user from each line, then count
optionB: Count the lines, then remove duplicates
optionC: Remove duplicate lines, then count
optionD: Extract the user from each line, remove duplicates, then count
correctAnswerText: Extract the user from each line, remove duplicates, then count
explanation: Deduplication has to come between extraction and counting. Removing duplicate whole lines leaves a user appearing under different remaining text more than once.

prompt: A team wants a log file both captured to disk and visible on screen as it runs. Redirecting sends the output to one destination instead of the other rather than to both. Which approach fits?
optionA: A stage that writes to a file and passes the same content onward
optionB: Redirect to the file, since it can be read afterwards
optionC: Leave it on the screen, since it can be copied out
optionD: Run the command twice, once for each destination
correctAnswerText: A stage that writes to a file and passes the same content onward
explanation: Redirecting is a move rather than a copy, so neither single destination meets the requirement. Running twice would produce two separate runs that need not agree.

prompt: A scheduled job must leave a record of everything that happened, including why it failed. Errors travel on a separate channel and are not captured by redirecting the ordinary output alone. What must the arrangement do?
optionA: Capture the ordinary output channel, which contains everything
optionB: Capture the error channel only, since failures are what matter
optionC: Capture both channels, since the reason for a failure travels on the error channel
optionD: Capture neither, and rely on the reported result value
correctAnswerText: Capture both channels, since the reason for a failure travels on the error channel
explanation: Capturing one channel leaves half the record missing, and which half depends on how the job went. The reported result value says that it failed and never why.

prompt: A team can build a report as one long pipeline of eight stages, or as a script with named intermediate steps. The pipeline is shorter to write and must be understood and modified by people joining the team throughout the year. The report will be modified repeatedly by people who did not write it. Which fits?
optionA: The pipeline, since it is shorter
optionB: The named steps, since the work is maintenance by people who did not write it
optionC: The pipeline, since fewer intermediate files are created
optionD: Either, since the two produce the same report
correctAnswerText: The named steps, since the work is maintenance by people who did not write it
explanation: Both produce the same report, so correctness cannot decide it. Eight anonymous stages have to be reconstructed from scratch by every reader.

prompt: A team must process a file too large to fit in memory. One approach reads the whole file into memory and sorts it; another passes it through a chain of stages, each handling a line at a time. The file is larger than the memory available and a chain of stages holds only what it is currently processing. Which fits?
optionA: The in-memory sort, since sorting is faster in memory
optionB: Either, since both process the same file
optionC: The in-memory sort, with the file split into pieces first
optionD: The chain of stages, since it never holds the whole file at once
correctAnswerText: The chain of stages, since it never holds the whole file at once
explanation: The constraint is what has to be held simultaneously rather than what is processed in total. Splitting first is a real technique and reintroduces the work the chain avoids.

prompt: A data platform lets steps be chained, each consuming what the previous produced. A step in the middle needs a value that was present in the original input and removed by an earlier step. Each step sees only what its predecessor produced, and the value was removed before this step. What follows?
optionA: The value is unavailable to it, and an earlier step must carry it forward
optionB: The step can request the original input
optionC: The step can ask the platform for the missing value
optionD: The value is restored automatically when needed
correctAnswerText: The value is unavailable to it, and an earlier step must carry it forward
explanation: The described chain has the same isolation as a pipeline, and the same consequence. Anything a later step needs has to survive every step before it.

prompt: A processing framework reports success for a chain when the final step succeeds. A middle step fails, produces nothing, and the final step succeeds on the empty input. The final step succeeded on an empty input and the chain is judged by the final step alone. What does the reported success mean?
optionA: That every step in the chain succeeded
optionB: That the chain produced correct output
optionC: Only that the last step ran without error, which an empty input allowed it to do
optionD: That the middle step recovered from its failure
correctAnswerText: Only that the last step ran without error, which an empty input allowed it to do
explanation: Judging a chain by its last step hides failures upstream, exactly as a pipeline can. Checking each step, or checking that the output is non-empty, is what closes the gap.

prompt: A build system chains tasks so that each consumes the previous output. A team adds a task that writes a report to the screen and passes nothing onward. Each task consumes what the previous produced, and this one produces nothing. What happens to the tasks after it?
optionA: They receive the report that was written to the screen
optionB: They receive nothing, so the chain effectively ends there
optionC: They receive the output of the task before it
optionD: They fail with an error about the missing input
correctAnswerText: They receive nothing, so the chain effectively ends there
explanation: Writing to the screen is not the same as passing something on, and the chain carries only what is passed. A task meant to observe without interrupting has to pass its input through unchanged.

prompt: A team must decide whether to build a transformation as one large step or as five small ones chained together. The five would each be independently testable and would pass data between them; the one large step would hold everything internally. Five chained steps can each be tested on their own, while one large step can only be tested end to end. Which fits a system that must be verified in detail?
optionA: The one large step, since it has fewer moving parts
optionB: The one large step, since passing data between steps is expensive
optionC: Either, since both produce the same transformation
optionD: The five chained steps, since each can be checked independently
correctAnswerText: The five chained steps, since each can be checked independently
explanation: Composability buys exactly what the requirement asks for, which is the ability to check the parts. Where verification did not matter, the single step and its lower overhead would be a reasonable choice.
